name: Google Cloud Spot VMs: up to 91% off, no SLA, and explicitly excluded from committed-use discounts
price_basis: PERCENT DISCOUNT CEILING, not a price. The Spot VM documentation states Spot VMs 'are available at much lower prices - up to 91% discounts' and, in the same paragraph, that 'Compute Engine might preempt Spot VMs at any time to reclaim resources'. price_usd carries the 91 (percent), which is the only number the page publishes. OBSERVATION DATE: the figure above was observed/listed on 2026-10-04 unless a different date is stated inline; treat it as needing re-verification once it is more than a quarter old. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
The GCP spot documentation is unusually explicit about four limitations that together make the headline discount unbankable, and each is quoted from the page. (1) NO SLA: Spot VMs 'are not covered by any Service Level Agreement and are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA'. (2) NO LIVE MIGRATION: 'Spot VMs can't live migrate' - so a spot instance cannot be evacuated onto on-demand capacity when it is preempted. (3) NO COMMITMENT DISCOUNT: the page states that 'credits for Compute Engine don't apply to Spot VMs', which is the same mutual-exclusion that the pricing page states explicitly for both Spot and preemptible VMs against CUDs and SUDs. This is the single most common error in spot cost models - multiplying a spot rate by a commitment discount. (4) FINITE AND ZONE-LOCAL: 'Spot VMs are finite Compute Engine resources, so they might not always be available', and availability 'varies based on Compute Engine usage'. On interruption mechanism: Compute Engine either STOPS (default) or DELETES the VM depending on the termination action you set, and 'The probability that Compute Engine preempts Spot VMs is generally low, but might vary from day to day and from zone to zone depending on current conditions'. GCP publishes spot pricing per instance type in its VM pricing table and, unlike AWS, states the discount percentage up front - which makes GCP the easier of the two to reason about and the easier to overestimate.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null - correct and not a gap. A token-priced serverless API is provisioned on request, so there is no lead time to publish; the binding constraint when a model is at capacity is provider-side queuing and any per-account concurrency limit, which this repo records in notes where a vendor publishes one (see the DeepSeek concurrency figures already here). Deliberately NOT recorded: any 'model capacity lead time' estimate, because vendors publish none and the SEO 'GPU lead time' numbers that circulate do not apply to a rented endpoint. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
